industry: Restaurants, QSR, pizza, cafes, catering, food trucks
words_and_claims_to_avoid: 'THE BEST pizza in town' (GOLD-restaurants-food-009/043) is usually puffery and allowed; specific objective claims ('#1 rated', 'award-winning', 'voted best') need a real source cited
'Free' items that require buying something at an inflated price (16 CFR 251); state the purchase requirement clearly
'Was $X now $Y' unless $X was the real regular price (16 CFR 233)
Health/nutrition claims ('healthy', 'low fat', 'gluten-free') without meeting FDA definitions
'Taco Tuesday' is free to use (Taco John's abandoned its mark in 2023); other slogans may be trademarked: check
Alcohol promos ('free drink', 'unlimited', 'two-for-one', drink coupons) without checking state liquor rules
Gift-card bonus offers without Reg E promotional labeling
compliance_notes: FTC Free Guide (16 CFR 251): 'free with purchase' requires the purchased item at its regular price and conditions stated clearly up front.

Alcohol promotions are state-regulated (verified examples): Texas TABC rules restrict coupons/rebates on alcohol; North Carolina bans free drinks and limits happy-hour pricing; New York SLA prohibits free drinks and unlimited-drink specials; Indiana ATC restricts two-for-one drinks; California ABC regulates bar promotions. Check every state before putting a drink offer on a mailer.

FDA menu labeling (21 CFR 101.11) applies to chains with 20+ locations: take-out menus that customers can order from must show calories and the 2,000-calorie statement; FDA guidance says coupons and advertising flyers that aren't used to order generally aren't menus. A mailer that doubles as a full order menu may count.
Gift cards (Reg E 12 CFR 1005.20, verified): purchased cards valid at least 5 years; bonus/promotional cards exempt only if labeled 'promotional' on the front with expiry and fees.
Sweepstakes/prize promos by mail (39 USC 3001(k)): 'no purchase necessary' and 'a purchase will not improve your chances' clearly and conspicuously, plus rules, odds and prize values.
Comparative claims vs named competitors must be truthful (FTC s.5; Lanham Act).
Food photos should show the real dish as served (FTC s.5 deception); styled shots are fine, substitutions are not.
standing_rules: Emotion-agnostic: fear, joy, pride, relief are all options; the client chooses.
Every angle carries a sell-the-outcome line.
Unverified (agency-only) results are labeled; never quote them as fact on a card.

emotion_by_offer_conflicts.conflict: Multi-coupon walls (many gold cards) justified by 'more choice' vs the choice-overload ('jam study') claim that more options hurt
emotion_by_offer_conflicts.resolution: Neither wins on evidence: the Scheibehenne 2010 meta-analysis found an average choice-overload effect near zero. Default to one hero offer (roofing votes, cross-vertical) and test multi-coupon backs.

emotion_by_offer_conflicts.conflict: Vendor case rates (MMR-187 8.64%, MMR-403 19.42%) vs no verified benchmarks
emotion_by_offer_conflicts.resolution: Treat as agency-only unverified; never quote to clients as expected results.

emotion_by_offer_conflicts.conflict: Drink offers in gold examples vs state alcohol rules
emotion_by_offer_conflicts.resolution: Law wins: food-only offers by default; drink offers only after a state check.
